Fourier Series Decomposition — Spatial Waves from Momentum States

About This Simulation

This interactive visualization demonstrates how complex waveforms can be constructed by summing simple sine waves — the core idea behind Fourier series.

Choose a square wave, sawtooth wave, Gaussian in a box, or double Gaussian and adjust the number of terms (N). The top panel shows each individual sine component with its amplitude and frequency. The bottom panel overlays the partial Fourier sum (colored line) against the ideal target (dashed line).

The square and sawtooth waves have discontinuities whose coefficients decay as 1/n, producing the Gibbs phenomenon (~9% overshoot even as N→∞). The Gaussian modes' coefficients decay super-exponentially, so convergence is dramatically faster. The double Gaussian breaks the single Gaussian's mid-box symmetry, activating even-n harmonics — compare the two regimes by switching wave types.

The equation bar at the top displays the current partial sum formula up to N terms.
Individual Components

Guided Inquiry

1 · Sines into a shape

Here’s the big idea: a Fourier series builds a waveform out of pure sine waves whose frequencies are whole multiples of one fundamental. The strip above shows you each harmonic on its own with its amplitude, and the plot below draws the sum of the first N of them against the target it’s aiming at.

2 · A vertical drop

Let’s start with the trickiest shape of all. The target is a square wave: it holds at +1, then falls instantly to −1. Yet every sine in the sum is smooth and continuous. What do you think — as more harmonics are added, what happens at that drop?

3 · The spike beside the jump

Now look closely beside the drop: a narrow spike of overshoot still stands on each side of it. Suppose you take N from 12 to 30 — nearly three times the harmonics. What’s your guess? The height of that spike will…

4 · A target with no edge

Now let’s swap the jump for something gentle. Thirty harmonics are in the sum; the n-th carries amplitude 4/(πn), so the last is a fifty-ninth of the first. Replace the square wave with a smooth Gaussian bump — no jump anywhere. How many of the thirty do you think will then carry appreciable amplitude?

5 · Sharper in space

Here’s where the quantum story comes in. On [0, L] the harmonics sin(nπx/L) are the stationary states of a particle confined to a box of width L, and n fixes the size of its momentum, though not its direction. Now narrow the bump: take σ/L from 0.10 to 0.02. What do you expect? The range of harmonics with appreciable amplitude…

The Physics

Fourier series · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

Almost any repeating shape can be built by adding sine waves whose frequencies are whole multiples of one base frequency, even a square wave with its sharp jumps. This sim adds the sines one at a time, so you can see how many it takes to match a target and what the sum looks like along the way.

What you'll learn

  • How each sine's amplitude is calculated, and why the amplitudes do not depend on one another.
  • How the quality of the match depends on the number of terms N and on the shape of the target.
  • What these sines are for a particle in a box.
  • How the width of a bump relates to the sines it needs.
The sim's two panels at N = 3: the three terms above, their sum below, against the dashed square-wave target.

What's on screen

  • Individual Components (top strip): one card per term, with its formula, its amplitude and its curve. Scroll sideways when N is large.
  • Dashed target: the shape being matched.
  • Partial sum (blue to pink curve): the N terms added together.
  • Sweeping line and dot: a marker that moves along the sum. It changes nothing.
  • Equation bar: the sum written out. For the square and sawtooth it shows the first six terms, then ⋯.
See itChoose the square wave with N = 3. Watch for: three cards in the strip, and below them one curve, their sum, roughly following the dashed square wave.

03

Where the sine waves come from

Every term is a sine whose frequency is a whole multiple of one base frequency. Two different ones, multiplied together and integrated over the range, give zero:

For the square and sawtooth read L = π (the terms are sin nx). For the Gaussians L = 1.

So each amplitude can be found on its own: multiply the target by that one sine and integrate. The sim does these sums for you and only adds the results:

The two jumpy targets, in the sim's own indexing.

The square wave uses odd harmonics only, so N counts terms, not harmonics. Term k carries n = 2k + 1: at N = 3 the terms are n = 1, 3, 5.

Key idea. Each amplitude depends only on its own n, never on N. Changing N adds or removes cards and leaves the others as they were.
See itSquare wave at N = 3, then N = 6. Watch for: the first three cards (A = 1.2732, 0.4244, 0.2546) unchanged when three more cards appear.
04

What a jump costs

A jump is a vertical edge, and smooth sines can imitate it only by piling up. The square-wave amplitudes fall slowly, A = 4/(nπ), and N terms reach n = 2N − 1.

  • The last card is 1/(2N − 1) of the first: 1/11 at N = 6, and still 1/59 (1.7%) at N = 30.
  • The slope of the sum at the jump (x = 0) is exactly 4N/π: 3.8 at N = 3, 38 at N = 30. It grows without limit as N does, which is how smooth curves approach a vertical edge.
  • The sawtooth has the same 1/n fall, with every n present and alternating signs. Its jump is at x = π.
See itSquare wave at N = 6, with the strip scrolled along. Watch for: the amplitudes sliding from A = 1.2732 down to only 0.1157 at the last card, n = 11.
05

The spike beside the jump stays

Just beside each jump the sum overshoots the target. More terms squeeze that spike towards the jump but do not lower it.

The square-wave sum near the jump at x = π, at N = 12 and N = 30.

The peak is 1.1796 at N = 12 and 1.1791 at N = 30. It tends to (2/π)∫₀^π (sin t / t) dt = 1.17898, so the overshoot settles at 8.95% of the jump (the jump is 2, from −1 to +1). The peak sits a distance π/2N from the jump.

Away from the jump the sum does converge to the target, because the spike keeps moving in. Right at the jump it never converges evenly. This is the Gibbs phenomenon. The sawtooth tends to the same limit at its jump, more slowly.

See itSquare wave at N = 12, then N = 30. Watch for: the spike beside each jump about as tall at N = 30 as at N = 12, only narrower.
06

What a smooth target needs

A Gaussian bump has no jump, and its coefficients fall much faster than 1/n:

The two Gaussian targets, as the sim computes them. L = 1.

The exponential factor is itself a Gaussian in n. It falls to 1/e at nₑ = √2 L/(πσ), and beyond about that n the cards are flat.

σ/Lnₑof 30 coefficients, above 1% of the largest
0.251.82
0.104.55
0.0222.515

Symmetry decides which n appear. The single bump is symmetric about L/2 and the even sines are antisymmetric about it, so their coefficients are exactly zero. Two bumps at L/4 and L/2 break that symmetry: n = 2, 6, 10 … carry weight, while n = 4, 8, 12 … stay exactly zero.

N σ/L

These sliders move the sim too. σ/L matters only for the Gaussian targets.

See itA Gaussian at σ/L = 0.10 with N = 30. Watch for: the n = 2 and n = 4 cards flat on zero, and the sum already sitting on the dashed bump.
See itTwo Gaussians at σ/L = 0.05 with N = 30. Watch for: the n = 2 card now showing a real curve (b₂ = 0.2386) while n = 4 stays flat.
07

The same series in a box

On [0, L] the terms sin(nπx/L) are the stationary states of a particle in an infinite square well, with energy Eₙ = n²π²ħ²/2mL². Read the bump as an unnormalised wavefunction ψ(x) = Σ bₙ sin(nπx/L). Then bₙ² is the weight on level n, and the probability of finding Eₙ is bₙ² divided by the sum of all the bₘ².

Each sine is an equal mix of a right-moving and a left-moving wave. So n fixes the size of the momentum, |p| = nπħ/L, but not its direction, and ⟨p⟩ = 0.

Coefficients bₙ/b₁ at two widths. The dashed line marks nₑ.

A narrower bump in x needs more levels, so its momentum is spread wider. For a Gaussian with σ ≪ L:

Δx is the spread of |ψ|², and Δp is the spread of the momentum.
See itA Gaussian at N = 30: σ/L = 0.10, then 0.02. Watch for: the strip scrolling past curved cards much farther out in n at σ/L = 0.02, every other card.
08

Where it matters

  • Sound. An ideal square-wave tone contains odd harmonics only, with amplitudes falling as 1/n: the series of the square wave here.
  • Imaging. An MRI scan measures only a finite range of spatial frequencies, which truncates the series. Sharp edges in the image then show ringing beside them, the Gibbs (or truncation) artefact.
  • Quantum states. Expanding a state in energy eigenstates is this same calculation, and the trade-off between width in x and spread in p is the uncertainty relation.
Go deeper: what the series captures, and where the sim's formulas stop
  • For the square wave, N terms carry (8/π²) Σ 1/(2k+1)² of the mean square: 81.1% at N = 1, 93.3% at N = 3, 99.3% at N = 30. The power converges even though the spike stays.
  • The Gaussian formulas assume σ ≪ L. Up to σ/L = 0.15 they agree with the exact box integral to within 0.0003. At σ/L = 0.25 they do not: b₅ is 0.0006 in the sim and 0.0279 exactly.
09

Summary

In one line. A Fourier series builds a shape from sines. A jump needs many terms and keeps an overshoot of 8.95% of the jump; a smooth bump needs few, and a narrower bump needs more.

Key points

  • Each amplitude is found on its own, so N only adds terms.
  • At a jump the amplitudes fall as 1/n; the spike narrows but keeps its height.
  • For a Gaussian the coefficients fall like a Gaussian in n, reaching 1/e at nₑ = √2 L/(πσ).
  • In a box the terms are energy states; a narrower bump needs more of them (ΔxΔp = ħ/2 for σ ≪ L).

Common mix-ups

  • "Add enough harmonics and the overshoot goes away." The spike narrows; its height stays at 8.95% of the jump.
  • "N is the highest harmonic." For the square wave the highest is n = 2N − 1.
  • "A sine in a box has a definite momentum." Only |p| = nπħ/L is definite; the sign is an equal mix.

Things to try on your own

  • Raise the square wave from N = 1, noting the n of each new card.
  • Choose Two Gaussians at σ/L = 0.05, N = 12, and list the cards that read exactly zero.
  • Choose Gaussian at N = 30 and move σ/L from 0.25 to 0.02, noting how far along the strip the amplitudes stay sizeable.
